01 — How to read this

We are no longer measuring every grade against one number

A single 80% target treated a Nursery class and a Grade 10 board cohort as though the same score meant the same thing. From this review onwards each stage carries its own target, and every figure on this page is measured against the target for that stage.

Two changes to how the marks are calculated, agreed for this review: papers marked AB are excluded from every average — the student's own percentage, the subject average, and every section, grade, branch and group comparison. Students recorded absent for a paper are no longer counted as zero — each student's percentage is now calculated only on the papers they actually sat. Students who sat no paper at all are excluded from every average and listed separately in section 10. This is a fairer basis for comparison, and it moves most section figures upward compared with the earlier sheet.

Click any band to see the grades inside it.

Note for the meeting: Grade and Stage 5 sit in the 80% band and Grade and Stage 6 begin the 75% band. If the intention was for Grade 5 to fall in the 75% group instead, that is a one-line change and every figure on this page will update.

03 — The whole group on one screen

All — sections, coloured by distance from their own target

One square per section. Because each stage has its own target, the colour shows how far a section is from its target — not its raw score. A Grade 1 section at 78% is behind; a Grade 9 section at 78% is ahead.

Read across a row to see how a grade is doing everywhere. Read down a column to see one branch at every stage. Where a dark square sits beside a green one in the same row and column, the two sections share a grade, a branch and a paper — and that is the most useful conversation on this page.

04 — Branch and grade

Each branch against its own blended target

Because branches teach different ranges of grades, they do not all carry the same target. A branch running mostly senior grades has a lower blended target than one with a large primary section — so the bar below each branch is set to its own mix, and the branches are genuinely comparable.

05 — The most useful finding in this data

What is already working, in our own classrooms

When two sections of the same grade, at the same branch, sitting the same paper, finish a long way apart, the difference is not the paper and it is usually not the intake. Something in the stronger room is working — and it costs nothing to share, because the teacher who did it is already on our staff.

This is the section of the review we would most like teachers to lead. The question is not why the lower section fell behind; it is what the stronger section did in the four weeks before the paper that we can all copy.

Click any row to compare the two sections side by side, subject by subject.
06 — Reading the pattern

Four different situations that look identical on a mark sheet

A low average can mean four quite different things, and each one calls for a different response. Sending the wrong response wastes the weeks we have before PT-2 — a whole-class re-teach when only six students needed help, or individual remediation when the entire class missed a topic.

These labels come from the marks alone. They are a prompt to look, never a judgement on a teacher. Before any of them is acted on, it should be checked against what the teacher already knows about that room.

Sections in each pattern

Filtered by the controls at the top of the page

Please read these fairly. A section can be down because a teacher was on leave, because the group was re-formed in April, because the paper ran long, or because two children missed half of it. None of that is visible in a spreadsheet. Every flag on this page is a question for the room, not an answer about it.

07 — Subjects

Where the subject picture points to a shared fix

Marks are converted to a percentage of each paper's own maximum, so a 15-mark Stage 5 paper and a 40-mark Grade 10 paper can sit in the same table. A subject weak at one branch is a delivery question for that branch. A subject weak at all four is a curriculum, pacing or paper-setting question, and it belongs with the subject HODs rather than with individual teachers.

Click a subject to see every section where it needs attention.
08 — The board year

Grade 10, section by section, inside each branch

Grade 10 gets its own review for one reason: it is the only cohort with no further year to recover in. The target for this grade is 75%, and the comparison that matters is within the branch — the sections sitting the same paper with the same teachers and the same seven weeks left.

Click any section for the full file.
09 — Getting there

What reaching target actually requires

Asking every child to gain the whole shortfall is not a plan. These four movements are modelled on the real student marks, so we can see which one is worth the term's effort — and be honest with each other about what a single term can and cannot deliver.

Change the unit to model each branch separately.
10 — Attendance and records

The part we can fix this week without teaching anything

— students have a record in the result sheet but no marks in any subject. They are now excluded from every average on this page rather than counted as zero. A further — students sat some papers but not all; their percentage is now calculated on the papers they actually sat.

The same rule runs through every figure on this dashboard. A paper marked AB is excluded from that student's percentage, from the subject average, from the section, grade, branch and group averages, and from every comparison between them. Nothing on this page is depressed by a paper that was never sat.

Neither group is a teaching problem. Both are records that need closing before PT-2, so that the next review compares like with like — and so that no teacher is asked to explain a number that was never theirs.
